newsitem.title: MEXICO: Lockheed Martin sees opportunity in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed Martin sees opportunity in Mexico.

text.p: Whether it be in the war on drugs or the privatization of telecommunications, airports and sea ports, Mexico is a land of opportunity for U.S. aerospace and high-tech giant Lockheed Martin, company officials said.
That's why some of the top company brass is in Mexico to participate in Aeroexpo '97, an international aviation trade show and convention that runs through this weekend.

"There's been a move toward setting up primary radars on the West Coast of Mexico so that narcotics traffickers coming up from South America will be visible," John Rougas, marketing manager for the Lockheed Martin subsidiary known as Ocean, Radar & Sensor Systems, told Reuters at the Lockheed Martin exhibit in the Acapulco Convention Center.
Rougas pointed to a poster of the TPS-117, a highly advanced radar unit mounted on a military-style truck that he said would be ideal for fighting the drug trafficking.

"We're very interested in pursuing the applications where a highly transportable radar like the TPS-117 is needed to provide the range and weather performance that's required in the mountainous regions of Mexico to counter narcotics trafficking," he said.
Rougas said the Mexican government was interested in such devices but conceded that they cost "a lot of money."

Frank Simpson, Lockheed Martin's vice president for Latin America, told Reuters that Mexico offers an array of opportunities for some of Lockheed Martin's nearly 100 subsidiaries, largely because of Mexican privatizations.

Since the former state telephone company Telmex, privatized in 1990, was opened to competition this year, Lockheed Martin, which builds and launches satellites, has positioned itself in the sector, Simpson said.

With airports due to be sold off, Lockheed Martin will bid on some of those through its Airport Group International subisidiary, which seeks to manage and operate airports throughout Latin America where other privatizations are taking place, he said.

But even if Airport Group International doesn't win a bid, Lockheed Martin will be ready to offer air traffic control systems and other hardware needed to improve the infrastructure through Ocean, Radar & Sensor Systems.
That same subisdiary also seeks to play a role in the privatization of Mexican sea ports, company officials said.
Simpson said Lockheed Martin remained highly interested in the airport privatizations even though they have been delayed and other privatizations have been set back for political reasons.
Any day now, the government is due to publish a long-awaited scheme for selling off its airports considered key to the privatization process.

"It has taken a long time in Mexico. We started to follow this process here maybe five years ago when this initially started," Simpson said. "It's a complex situation. But I think the telecommunications area is paving the way. It's all been done under the SCT (Communications and Transport Ministry) and been a good experience for them."
